item.content:encoded:
Six partners have signed an agreement to coordinate efforts to eradicate brown tree snakes from Islan Dåno’, also known as Cocos Island.

The agreement was signed Tuesday during the 2026 annual Brown Tree Snake Technical Working Group public meeting. It brings together the Guam Department of Agriculture’s Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources; the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s Pacific Islands Fish and Wildlife Office; the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Wildlife Services; Friends of Island Dåno; Tåno, Tåsi yan Todu, and the Malesso’ Mayor’s Office.

The effort aims to completely remove the invasive snakes from Cocos Island and protect the island’s native wildlife, including the ko’ko’ or Guam Rail. The Guam rail was considered extinct in the wild before birds were released on Cocos Island.

Farron Taijeron, who coordinates the eradication project for Tåno, Tåsi, yan Todu, said the partnership is essential to making the project successful.

“The partnership is critical because no one can do everything alone,” Taijeron said. “So being able to work together, spread the load out among different people, different agencies, different partners, is really the only way to get success.”

The meeting also included updates on brown tree snake prevention, detection and control efforts across Guam and the neighboring islands.

Federal agencies, territorial departments and community partners shared updates on funding, research, inspection programs and ongoing efforts to keep the invasive snakes from spreading through cargo and transportation routes.

Presentations covered snake control work at Guam’s ports, shipping facilities, power substations and military installations, as well as efforts in the CNMI and Hawaii to inspect incoming cargo and respond to reported sightings.

Researchers also discussed rapid response operations in the CNMI during 2026, including a response in Saipan after a reported snake sighting and another in Rota after two snakes were detected. One snake was recovered dead in cargo, and a juvenile snake was reported as captured and killed. Other presentations focused on emerging detection methods, including environmental DNA, and research into improving snake traps and control strategies.

The project combines agency-led snake control with community participation. The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Wildlife Services resumed brown tree snake control work on Cocos Island in fiscal 2026 and has supported community removal efforts.

Friends of Islan Dåno’ has also involved nearly 500 community volunteers in the effort.

Sustaining the project will require continued coordination and funding. The Guam Dept. of Agriculture director, Chelsa Muna, said funding has been released to allow the program to continue, but the department hopes to secure additional support. Muna also said the department is working to expand its captive breeding program for the Guam rail, with the hope of eventually releasing more birds on Cocos Island.

Taijeron said successful eradication would be a first worldwide. He emphasized that the goal is to completely remove the snakes from the island, rather than simply reduce their numbers.

The memorandum formalizes the partners’ shared commitment to the eradication effort. The work is intended to help protect Cocos Island’s native and endangered species and support the long-term recovery of its ecosystem.

item.content:encoded:
Del. Kimberlyn King-Hinds said she remains in regular communication with Department of Homeland Security leadership following the suspension of the CNMI's Economic Vitality and Security Travel Authorization Program, or EVS-TAP, emphasizing the need to balance federal security concerns with the commonwealth's economic realities.

In a statement, King-Hinds said she has sought a better understanding of the issues that led DHS to suspend the program and has stressed the potential impact the decision could have on the CNMI economy.

"Good public policy requires a full understanding of the interests being pursued and the consequences, both intended and unintended, of the decisions being made," she said. "That is especially important when those decisions affect an economy already facing tremendous challenges."

King-Hinds said she met last week with U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services Deputy Director James Kernochan to discuss the concerns behind the suspension and explore possible steps federal and CNMI officials could take to address those issues.

According to King-Hinds, the meeting focused on identifying measures that could satisfy DHS concerns while helping restore visitor arrivals.

"It was a frank and productive discussion, and I appreciate Commissioner Scott and Deputy Director Kernochan taking the time to hear our concerns and work through the issues with us," she said.

She also thanked Scott for continuing the dialogue and expressed optimism about future collaboration.

DHS suspended EVS-TAP effective Oct. 30, citing national security and immigration enforcement concerns.

The program allowed eligible Chinese nationals to travel directly to the CNMI without obtaining a U.S. visa after undergoing pre-screening and advance authorization.

Federal officials said the suspension was prompted by vulnerabilities involving travelers from China, including visa overstays, unauthorized employment and other abuses of federal immigration programs.

Tourism stakeholders and local officials have expressed concern that the loss of EVS-TAP could further hinder the commonwealth's economic recovery amid ongoing challenges facing the visitor industry.

item.title: Brown Tree Snake Working Group to sign agreement to eradicate snakes from Cocos Island
item.description: Members of the Brown Tree Snake Technical Working Group are preparing to sign a memorandum of understanding aimed at eradicating invasive brown tree snakes from Islan Dåno’, also known as Cocos Island. The signing is scheduled for Nov. 17, during the group’s annual public meeting at the Hilton Guam Resort and Spa. The agreement formalizes six years of efforts to eliminate the snakes from the islan
item.content:encoded:
Members of the Brown Tree Snake Technical Working Group are preparing to sign a memorandum of understanding aimed at eradicating invasive brown tree snakes from Islan Dåno’, also known as Cocos Island.

The signing is scheduled for Nov. 17, during the group’s annual public meeting at the Hilton Guam Resort and Spa. The agreement formalizes six years of efforts to eliminate the snakes from the island through collaboration among local conservation organizations, nonprofit groups, the Government of Guam, and federal agencies.

A breeding population of brown tree snakes was discovered on Dåno’ in 2020, prompting independent efforts to remove the invasive species. Organizers say the goal is to achieve complete eradication, which would mark the first successful removal of an invasive snake from an island anywhere in the world.

Dåno’ is home to the only wild population of ko’ko’, or Guam rails, which disappeared from Guam due to brown tree snake predation. The snakes have had significant ecological and economic impacts on Guam and remain a threat to neighboring islands.

The annual meeting will also feature updates on brown tree snake research, management, and eradication efforts. Organizers say this year’s work has been particularly demanding following three typhoons and two brown tree snake sightings on Rota after Typhoon Bavi.

The public meeting runs from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with the memorandum signing scheduled for 12:20 p.m. in the Micronesian Room at the Hilton Guam Resort and Spa.

The event is free and open to the public.

item.title: Questions about FAA funding roil Capitol Hill after nationwide ground stop
item.description: Commercial air traffic is just about back to normal, three days after a communications meltdown that led the FAA to ground planes from taking off across the country. item.content:encoded:
Commercial air traffic is just about back to normal, three days after a communications meltdown that led the FAA to ground planes from taking off across the country. It took several days to untangle it all, leaving people stranded in airports coast to coast. And now there are big questions about what happened - questions from government watchdogs, from Congress. And the Trump administration is trying to use the moment to lobby for billions of dollars to upgrade the country's air traffic control infrastructure. With us to talk about it all are NPR's Joel Rose, who covers transportation, and congressional reporter Sam Gringlas. Hey everybody.

DETROW: So, Joel, you and I were talking as this all kind of unfolded on Friday. Here we are a few days later. How are things going with flights around the country?

ROSE: Much better than when we spoke on Friday.

ROSE: I'm happy to tell you. It's not perfect out there. There are plenty of delays. United Airlines in particular had an unrelated issue with its technology that delayed flights this afternoon for about an hour. But cancellations overall are way down. They are in the low hundreds today, not the thousands that we were seeing on Friday and also on Saturday. So basically, this looks a lot like a normal Monday. And that's a good sign, especially with the busy Thanksgiving travel season right around the corner.

DETROW: Yeah. Have we learned any more about what exactly happened? - because that was one of the confusing things in the moment, even as administration officials started to speak. There were just so many questions.

ROSE: Well, we're getting a clearer picture, but there are still some things we don't know. The FAA says that the problem seemed to originate with a longtime contractor that was doing work to replace older copper wire with new fiber optic cable. And that apparently disrupted FAA communication and radar equipment across a big part of the country and forced the agency to issue this rare nationwide ground stop that went on for over four hours, ultimately, on Friday.

The exact details are still under investigation, but there were some warnings about exactly this scenario in a report that was released just in September by the General Accountability Office. The GAO report noted that the administration has been speeding up the timeline of modernization work that was already underway, including on this exact telecommunications network that apparently failed on Friday. I talked earlier today with Kevin Walsh, the director of the GAO's Information Technology and Cybersecurity Team, and the lead on this report.

KEVIN WALSH: They are basically buying speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and the potential for disruptions in the national airspace. It increases the risk of outages, especially when dealing with these older systems which are prone to failure.

ROSE: Walsh says there is widespread agreement that this modernization work is necessary, that these air traffic control systems are very old, definitely in need of replacement. But the GAO report says doing this work on an accelerated timeline comes with risks, not just for operations but also for major cost overruns if there is not careful planning and budgeting.

ROSE: Something I mentioned at the top is that the Trump administration is asking Congress for more money in this moment. Here is President Trump today.

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We've been working with Congress to try and get the money. I think the one good thing that comes out of it, I'm sure Congress now will give us the money to fix it.

DETROW: So, Sam, tell us what the case is for this money that the administration is making.

GRINGLAS: Yeah. So Trump there is blaming decades of inaction over multiple administrations for what happened on Friday. And the Trump administration says this Congress is at fault for not forking over more money that they've been asking for. The day before this ground stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy actually wrote to Congress re-upping a request for an additional $30 billion, including $10 billion for air traffic control modernization. And then, after this ground stop on Friday, Duffy's ask grew to $50 billion. And House Speaker Mike Johnson, at least, has said he wants to get this money approved in the lame duck session of Congress.

DETROW: We heard the president there talking like this is a done deal. Many things in this Congress, Sam, have not been a done deal.

GRINGLAS: Yeah. Yeah. Well, Democrats have balked at allocating more money at all because they say Congress has already given the administration plenty of funding. Here's Democratic Congressman James Walkinshaw of Virginia.

JAMES WALKINSHAW: If money is the barrier, I'll support more money to modernize the air traffic control system. They haven't presented a plan or demonstrated that money is the barrier here, and money or lack of money was not the cause of Friday's incident.

GRINGLAS: And it is true that Congress has already provided the administration $14.5 billion to modernize FAA systems through the annual bipartisan transportation budget and also through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Republicans passed last year. Democrats say, of that money, some $9 billion remains unspent. Congresswoman Rosa DeLauro, who is the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee in the House, said in a statement that Cabinet heads need to take responsibility for mismanagement of funds. A handful of lawmakers have also said the administration, if they need more money, they should divert some of the billions of dollars Republicans have already allocated to ICE last year with few strings attached.

DETROW: Joel, going back to you, all of this comes amid a broader effort to improve air safety that came in the wake of that horrifying 2025 midair collision here in Washington, D.C. Can you put all of this into context for us?

ROSE: Yeah. That collision of a passenger jet and a U.S. Army Black Hawk helicopter killed 67 people last year, and it brought a lot of attention to the state of the air traffic control system. And that, along with some communication problems last year in Newark and other Eastern airports, is really what galvanized the Trump administration to begin pushing for more money to upgrade the system.

That midair collision also prompted a lot of safety recommendations from the National Transportation Safety Board. One thing, in particular, they called for is the wider use of a safety system that investigators say could have prevented the crash. The Senate unanimously approved a bill that would have required that system in all aircraft, but it stalled out in the House, where it came up just a few votes short after the Pentagon pulled its support at the last minute. Families of the victims of that midair collision want to see a compromise bill that could pass both the House and the Senate, and they are pushing for another vote during the lame duck session of Congress, and they will hold an event in Washington, D.C., tomorrow to push for their case.

DETROW: And, Sam, Democrats talking up oversight so much once they take back control in January. Could that extend to aviation safety?

GRINGLAS: Yeah, definitely - the FAA administrator, Bryan Bedford, is already scheduled to testify in Congress next month. But Democrats on the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee say they're already planning to bring back an investigation staff when they take power next year, and looking into the rollout of these upgrades is going to be a top priority.

DETROW: That is NPR congressional reporter Sam Gringlas, along with NPR transportation correspondent Joel Rose. Thanks to both of you.

ROSE: Thanks, Scott. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

item.title: California sues OpenAI over hacking risks
item.description: California sued OpenAI Monday, alleging that the frontier AI company failed to protect the public from its systems' advanced cyber capabilities. item.content:encoded:
California sued OpenAI Monday, alleging that the frontier AI company failed to protect the public from its systems' advanced cyber capabilities. The lawsuit stems from OpenAI's agents' attack on open-source software platform Hugging Face over the summer but also touches on a wide range of other related incidents tied to the company's agents acting without authorization.

"Just because the technology is new or rapidly evolving doesn't mean the people behind it are above the law," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. "Whether it's a car or a toy, the law is simple: don't build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards." The lawsuit cited potential concerns about cyberattacks "on power grids, emergency infrastructure, hospital systems, and financial institutions."

In the complaint , California alleged that OpenAI misled the public about how unsafe its products are. The state said the company admitted to the attorney general's office that "it lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing."

That number is higher than what OpenAI has so far disclosed publicly and more than what outside researchers have independently discovered, but OpenAI has otherwise provided little information, California said. The state also accused OpenAI of poor security practices, stonewalling the state's investigation into the company and discouraging employees from speaking up about safety.

In a statement to NPR, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab" and that the company has "engaged—and will continue to engage—constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry."

After the most notorious of cyber incidents involving OpenAI's agents – the attack on Hugging Face over the summer – the company admitted that it did not monitor its agents in ways its own researchers deemed important. Since then, outside researchers as well as OpenAI itself have found more incidents in which AI agents have interacted with websites and communicated with each other on the internet in ways that OpenAI did not intend. The lawsuit mentions these events as well as other incidents that OpenAI started disclosing voluntarily to the public.

Other AI companies have also had to wrestle with their systems behaving in unexpected and undesirable ways. Anthropic and Meta have both said they found that their AI systems have hacked into places they shouldn't have. Major AI companies have since signed onto an agreement organized by the White House to develop AI responsibly, but the agreement is nonbinding.

Drawing from reports including from OpenAI's own disclosures, California alleges that the top AI company has engaged in unfair competition and created a public nuisance. It asked the court to stop the company from further engaging in such activities and order it to pay monetary damages.

item.title: If Robert Pattinson is James Bond, 007 needs to get a little weird
item.description: James Bond has been played by Sean Connery, Roger Moore, Daniel Craig and now British actor Robert Pattinson. (SOUNDBITE OF MONTY NORMAN'S "THE JAMES BOND THEME")
item.content:encoded:
James Bond has been played by Sean Connery, Roger Moore, Daniel Craig and now British actor Robert Pattinson.

(SOUNDBITE OF MONTY NORMAN'S "THE JAMES BOND THEME")

PFEIFFER: Rumors had been flying about who will play 007 next, and Amazon shared the casting news today. Many people have opinions about this, and NPR critic Glen Weldon joins me now to talk about his. Hi, Glen.

PFEIFFER: What did you think when you heard this?

WELDON: I mean, it's an interesting choice. It's a bit puzzling too. I mean, Pattinson always seemed to me like a character actor who got stuck with a leading man's face, you know?

WELDON: His first big role, of course, was hunky teen heartthrob Cedric Diggory in the "Harry Potter" franchise. Then he went on to play a broody teen heartthrob vampire in the "Twilight" films. And he certainly got the looks of an old-school Hollywood leading man, you know, the facial symmetry, the cheek bones you could cut glass with. But he is kind of a weirdo, and I say that admiringly. If you see him in films like "The Lighthouse" or "The Odyssey" or "Mickey 17," where he plays different clones of himself, he really seems like somebody who likes to dig in and serve up big, quirky, offbeat performances. Like, here he is in "Mickey 17."

ROBERT PATTINSON: (As Mickey Barnes) The whole body printing and memory transplanting thing, to be honest, was so ridiculously ahead of its time that it caused so many, like, ethical fights and religious, blah, blah, blah, that it was actually banned on Earth, and they only allow it now in outer space for expendables like me.

WELDON: He's making a lot of big, weird choices in that movie. And that's not something anyone has ever said about a James Bond movie. That's the puzzling part. I mean, I think he'd make a great Bond villain, but he's going to be Bond.

PFEIFFER: So this is an actor whose career is a mixture of quirky indies, like the ones you just said, and then you have blockbuster franchises. I mean, he's our current live-action Batman. So when you envision Robert Pattinson as Bond, how do you think he'll do in this role?

WELDON: Well, you know, in interviews, Pattinson has talked about how uncomfortable he got with the kind of fame that the "Twilight" series kind of thrust upon him. You got the sense that he was chafing against the confines that a role in a big Hollywood franchise comes with, but he keeps going back to franchises. Now, I suspect that's just the way the world works now. Blockbusters still drive the economy of Hollywood, and he plays a Batman or a James Bond, so he can go off between those pictures and make something like "Primetime" this year, where he played "To Catch A Predator" host Chris Hansen with a hilarious, kind of lizard-like intensity. So it's a one for them, one for me. That's just the new normal.

PFEIFFER: When this casting announcement was made today, the producer said that they see Pattinson as the perfect Bond for our times. Of course they might say that. But what do you think they mean by our times?

PFEIFFER: And what do you think this means for where they want to take the 007 franchise?

WELDON: I mean, it's hard to say. James Bond is one of those roles that so much of it is on rails - right? - just kind of comes with the tux. What do we know about him? He's hot. He's suave. He gets beat up. He's got cars, gadgets and women.

WELDON: This character is enough of a cipher that an actor can bring pretty much anything they want, and they won't hurt the brand - because it is a brand. I mean, it's more commercial property than an acting role. You could argue that the character itself is kind of a dinosaur, a holdover from a past era of Hollywood, but these movies do well. They're packed with action and stunts and cool-looking cars. They do get butts in seats. And so even though, spoiler, Sacha, they did kill off James Bond in "No Time To Die" back in 2021 - the ironically titled "No Time To Die" - they were never going to let him stay dead. I mean, the shareholders wouldn't allow that.

PFEIFFER: So, Glen, in your perfect critic's dream world, what kind of James Bond will Robert Pattinson be?

WELDON: I don't know. I hope we see some of Robert Pattinson the kind of squirrely character actor peeking out from behind the gun once in a while. I mean, let's let Bond get freaky and offbeat and idiosyncratic. Certainly the Bond in Ian Fleming's novels is a true sociopath, and the movies have always kind of sanded that down a bit. But now he's going to be played by an actor who always seemed to me like that kid back in high school who got a little too excited about dissecting the frog, you know?

WELDON: Something was off about that kid. And now that kid is all grown up, and he has a license to kill. I mean, I'd watch that movie.

PFEIFFER: Robert Pattinson as James Bond coming soon to theaters near us. That is Glen Weldon, a critic on NPR's Pop Culture Happy Hour podcast. Glen, thank you.

(SOUNDBITE OF MONTY NORMAN'S "THE JAMES BOND THEME") Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

item.title: Pilot and journalist says fault lines beginning to show in U.S. air travel
item.description: Flights are still delayed today after Friday's ground stop, the longest one since 9/11, and travelers or would-have-been travelers are trying to figure out if they'll be compensated for canceled flights. To help we called Kyle Potter. He is the executive director (ph) at Thrifty Traveler, a travel and flight deal website.
item.content:encoded:
Flights are still delayed today after Friday's ground stop, the longest one since 9/11, and travelers or would-have-been travelers are trying to figure out if they'll be compensated for canceled flights.

To help we called Kyle Potter. He is the executive director (ph) at Thrifty Traveler, a travel and flight deal website.

KYLE POTTER: If their flight was actually canceled by the airline, they would be entitled to a refund or to just be put on the next available flight.

DETROW: But if you decided to cut your losses and cancel your ticket yourself...

POTTER: The best you will get is a voucher to use with your airline. The reality is, is that air travel in the United States is basically the Wild West, and there are very few customer protections in place to get reimbursed when things go wrong.

PFEIFFER: With the country's busiest travel season starting in just a few days, we wondered whether there are ways to insulate yourself if more problems arise, weather-related or systemic.

DETROW: Potter says prepare for the worst, go into busy days with a backup plan and take the early flight.

POTTER: The best thing anybody can do, whether they're booking a flight soon or have the option of changing a flight over the holidays, is to take the first flight of the day, because that gives you the best shot at getting where you need to go on time. Because the longer the day goes on, the more problems snowball.

DETROW: And in worst-case scenarios, days like Friday make a good argument for booking travel insurance.

POTTER: If something does go wrong, that's going to make sure that you're not, you know, stuck holding the bag for hundreds, if not a thousand dollars or more in unexpected expenses.

PFEIFFER: Our next guest is a pilot and a journalist. One day before the nationwide ground stop, James Fallows published a cover story for The New York Times Magazine that now seems extremely prescient. It is headlined, "Is Air Travel Getting Less Safe?" Jim Fallows joins us now. Thank you for making time for us.

PFEIFFER: I want to start with the general disclaimer that we often hear that even getting in a car, which most of us do a lot, is far more dangerous than flying. So is it fair to say that, overall, flying in our airspace remain quite safe?

FALLOWS: Yes. And my story talks about the almost 16-year miraculous spread between 2009 and last year in which the U.S. had 10 million passenger journeys and onto airlines and zero fatalities from crashes. So there's been a consequential crash since then over the Potomac last year, but statistically, compared to anything else you do in your day, being on a U.S. airliner is the safest thing you can do.

PFEIFFER: And that crash last year was when a U.S. Army Blackhawk helicopter hit an American Eagle jet coming into Reagan Airport, and everyone in those aircraft died, almost 70 people.

FALLOWS: Yes. And that was one of those major tragedies from which the U.S. aviation system has tried to derive lessons. The mantra of aviation in the U.S. has been, no passenger should die for the same reason twice. If they can learn enough about what happened when people perish, then they can try to prevent that particular thing from happening in the future...

FALLOWS: ...And they've been very successful.

PFEIFFER: There is a key line in your article. It says over the past 22 months, the rate of airplane accidents and close calls have suggested a system under enormous strain. And you also talk about how, as we have heard over the past few days, aging equipment - we had someone on Morning Edition today say that oftentimes the equipment is older than the people using it - air traffic control understaffing, a deregulatory blitz that has removed some of the aviation safety net. So all of these things are coming together to extremely tax the system. Is that what's happening?

FALLOWS: Yes. And there is a good side to the agedness of the systems, which is that the FAA has had a long-held bias for better safe than sorry. It takes a much longer time to have equipment certified as being safe and reliable for the life and death consequences of managing air travel than in some other, say, in video games or something else, where if it goes down, then it's inconvenience but not worse than that. And that understandable bias by the FAA has been combined with a less-admirable bias in our system of government, which is that the investment it takes to make this system up to date and maintain it as being safe - their payoff period is long beyond the next election horizon of the people in Congress and in the White House who are making these choices.

PFEIFFER: You are tough on the Trump administration in your article. You specifically point out the Washington D.C. area crash last year, and you say that - in your words - the Trump administration has displayed an extraordinary unwillingness to learn new lessons from that crash. Do you feel like, under the Trump administration, the system has worsened because of things that this administration are doing?

FALLOWS: Everything in aviation is in the long term, and we won't know for a while what lessons this system has learned and not learned from the tragedy of last year and the inconvenience and the disruption of the last week. But there have been a number of worrisome, immediate indications. One is the FAA's track of very serious runway incursions. This sounds illogical, but the runway is the most dangerous place where an airplane can be, because the runways are so small and so many airplanes are competing to get there. And the ranking of the category A and category B runway incursions - that is the most serious - has been going up in the last year and a half.

Bad things do happen in aviation and have over the years. And the strength of the U.S. system has been when something goes wrong, they're very careful and systematic and nonpartisan and collaborative and transparent process of saying what happened, and how can we learn from that? It's not obvious that the administration has taken those lessons from the Potomac crash, and in the last couple of days, we've heard mainly partisan blaming of previous administrations.

PFEIFFER: I should note that the National Transportation Safety Board posted on social media - I assume you've see this - about your article. And it says contrary to the tone of the article, the NTSB appreciates the administration's continued support, which has provided the agency with the vital resources needed to accomplish our work. And as you also know, the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, is asking for $50 billion to modernize the air traffic control system. Two questions about Duffy. Do you agree that 50 billion is the right amount of money to fix this system, and would that amount fully fix the problem?

FALLOWS: So I will note that more than a year ago, you know, in the summer of last year, when the so-called Big Beautiful Bill was passed, it included $12 billion for modernizing of the air traffic control system. And the same Secretary Duffy said then that those $12 billion would be enough to modernize the system and to have it done largely by now. He said it would take a year and a half or two years or so to modernize it. So a year and a half ago, he was saying that one-quarter of that amount of money would be enough to do the job and have it mainly done by now.

PFEIFFER: What do you make of the quadrupling of the ask?

FALLOWS: I make that it is not carefully thought through, and I think that Congress would want to look carefully about how the money already allocated has been spent and for what, and why there's still this single point of failure, as we've had, which aviation does everything it can to avoid.

PFEIFFER: Is this a situation where things could get worse before they get better? And I don't necessarily mean crashes. I mean even airport mayhem becoming more often.

FALLOWS: I think the upshot of this particular episode is not likely to get worse in the short run. And probably, now that people know about this vulnerability, they'll avoid any kind of tinkering that would lead to a similar disruption. But I think the larger situation you can liken to the situation of earthquakes in California, my original homeland, where you can't predict day by day or even year by year what's going to happen, but you see the trends, you see where tension is building up. And so much as there are fault lines among the plates in California for earthquakes, I think we see the fault lines building up in our aviation system.

PFEIFFER: That is Jim Fallows. He's a pilot and a writer, and he has a Substack called Breaking the News. Thank you.

FALLOWS: Thank you, Sacha. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.
